findings.summary: THE FLOOR OF 4 DOES NOT KILL multipliedBy(2); it kills it about 40% of the time, and the comment's premise that the mutant 'measures EXACTLY 3' is false on this machine. MEASURED in the reviewer tree, every run forced with --rerun-tasks and every count read from TEST-binjava.sequencer.LocalSequencerRenewTest.xml, with a temporary println of fastRate/slowRate (removed afterwards; git diff empty at the end). Mutant `sleepFor(leases.renewInterval().multipliedBy(2))` in the 4-arg start: fastRate = 4, 3, 4, 4, 3 over five class-scoped runs -- failures 0, 1, 0, 0, 1 -- plus two full :sequencer:test runs (246 tests) at 1 failure then 0. Killed in 3 of 7 runs, survived in 4. The mutant is bimodal at 3/4 because 1000ms/300ms = 3.33, not 3. Clean honest values: 6 (three idle runs), 6 (two runs under 32 spinners on 20 cores), 7 (two runs at load average 123). multipliedBy(4) lands at 2 and dies every time. So the floor of 4 is NOT too tight for flake -- honest never went below 6 in seven runs, including at load 123, which answers the question the packet asked -- it is too LOOSE to be a detector: the mutant's upper mode sits exactly on it. The band that still survives is roughly 0.75x-2.22x, which at this class's own 3s/10s configuration includes the 2x that puts a 9s renew against a 10s TTL, i.e. M4.17's own defect reinstated. The second sequencer does not separate this case as the comment claims: under the 2x mutant slowRate = 0 in all five runs and the only bound on it is isLessThan(3L), so 0 passes. The same claim is restated in baselines/review.txt:131 ('The floor is 4 now') and is equally unsupported. NOT worth a third fix round on the same line unless the fix is the robust one: widening the measurement window from 1000ms to 2000ms puts honest at ~13 and the 2x mutant at ~6, so a floor of 9 separates them with margin on both sides for one extra second of wall time. A cheaper alternative is bounding slowRate BELOW as well -- honest was 1 in all seven clean runs including at load 123, and 0 in all five 2x runs -- but that leaves only one unit of honest margin, which is the shape of the problem being fixed.
findings.failure_scenario: A refactor writes sleepFor(leases.renewInterval().multipliedBy(2)) -- or any scaling in roughly 0.75x-2.22x -- at LocalSequencer.java's 4-arg start. The build is green on most runs, and on the run where it is red the failure looks like the timing flake the comment says it is not, so it is re-run and lands. In production a configured 9s/10s renew becomes 18s against a 10s TTL: every pod loses its term at each TTL and burns an epoch, which is exactly the defect M4.17 exists to remove and, per this task's own backlog row, what M4.16 shows turning into an I2 violation.

findings.summary: THE REPLACEMENT CLAIM IN THE drainPermits COMMENT IS ALSO NOT WHAT THE TREE DOES. It says that without the drain, the fence-on-IOException mutation 'still dies, but at awaitExpiryPast's twenty-second deadline instead of at the commit two lines below'. MEASURED, with the IOException catch in LocalSequencer.renewForever mutated to `fenced = true; return;` and every run forced with --rerun-tasks, counts and per-test times read from the result XML: (a) with the test exactly as staged, aStoreFAILUREDuringRenewDoesNotFenceAHealthyLeader fails at tickAndAwaitProcessed's SECOND assertion, 'the renewer processed the tick and came back round', at 5.07s and 5.04s -- not at seq.commit and not at awaitExpiryPast; (b) with `parked.drainPermits()` deleted as well, the identical assertion fails at 5.05s, 5.05s, 5.08s. Removing the drain costs nothing observable, because its only caller is line 291 and no `tick()` precedes it in that test, so no stale permit can exist there; the drain is defensive against a call pattern the tree does not have, which is fine, but the sentence that says what it 'costs, measured' describes neither of the two states. Also worth naming for its own sake: the assertion that actually catches the fence-on-IOException mutant is the ticker helper's liveness timeout, not the commit the test was written around, because the mutant returns from the renew loop and the rendezvous can never complete. The commit line does constrain the non-returning variant (`fenced = true` without the return), so the test is not weak -- the comment is.
findings.failure_scenario: A future session reads a 'measured' sentence, treats the 20s deadline as the live net for this mutation, and either shortens awaitExpiryPast or deletes the rendezvous believing the other one catches it -- the same disbelief-of-the-tool loop this task already recorded in M4.40. Second-order: this is the second consecutive round in which this comment states a measurement the tree does not support, which is non-negotiable 4's failure mode in prose rather than in code.
